newsitem.title: POLAND: BANK UNLIKELY TO SAVE POLISH GDANSK SHIPYARD.
newsitem.headline: BANK UNLIKELY TO SAVE POLISH GDANSK SHIPYARD.

text.p: Poland's bankrupt Gdansk shipyard, cradle of the Solidarity trade union, appeared to be heading for final collapse on Wednesday as a local bank said it was unlikely to grant the enterprise a crucial loan.

The loan, of between $120 and $150 million, would keep part of the yard's 5,000-strong workforce busy building five vessels for a German investor while the government and the yard would continue to seek an investor to save the business.

The German offer to sign a contract with the yard expires on Thursday and without it the company, operating under bankruptcy regulations since August with debts of 415 million zlotys ($148 million), would have little to do.
The workers, who suspended a protest campaign against the state-controlled yard's collapse last week, will receive wages from a special government fund only until mid-February.

Bank Gdanski , with which the firm's administrator has been trying to negotiate the loan, said on Wednesday that current cooperation on a contract to build one vessel had been unsatisfactory and had discouraged the bank from further deals with the shipyard.
"Bank Gdanski has not launched a credit procedure, has not accepted the outline for creating a banking consortium and has not asked the treasury for guarantees," it said in a statement.
"Bank Gdanski is a commercial financial institution, which is inclined to participate in any venture, in which economic effectiveness and the risk level are acceptable," it added.
The government reiterated on Wednesday that the only way it could help the shipyard was through extending partial credit guarantees, but only if a bank first agreed to a loan.
"If the government receives an application for guarantees, it will consider it," government spokeswoman Aleksandra Jakubowska told a news conference.

But the yard's administrator, Wieslaw Szaj, said he still thought the treasury, a bank and the yard could set up a temporary venture that would keep business alive during the hunt for a strategic investor.

Meanwhile, Gdansk workers and Solidarity trade union officials met to discuss whether to resume their protest, which involved a hunger strike by seven people and a sit-in by 300 inside the provincial governor's headquarters.
Many unionists and politicians allege the government, which has helped other state-owned enterprises, is refusing aid for the shipyard because it is a nest of political opposition.
Solidarity, which toppled communism in 1989, is leading an electoral bloc which hopes to defeat the co-ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) in next year's general election.

The government accuses previous managements of signing unprofitable contracts and bringing bankruptcy on the shipyard -- where 17 years ago Lech Walesa set up Solidarity, the then Soviet bloc's first free trade union. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
